questions.challenge_mechanism: Every option in the cluster is the exact result of one defensible reading of the same graph, so nothing can be answered by recognising a formula. The cluster turns on three separations the candidate has to hold at once: the area under the graph is not the peak force times the distance; the accumulated net work is not the applied work; and the point of greatest force is not the point of greatest kinetic energy. The last of these is the pivot, because the friction is a constant that never appears on the graph and so is easily left out of the comparison altogether.
questions.question: A trolley of mass 3.0 kg starts from rest at $x = 0$ and is pushed along a straight, level track by a force whose magnitude varies with the distance $x$ exactly as shown in the figure. The force rises uniformly from zero at the start to 6.0 N at $x = 2.0$ m, stays at 6.0 N until $x = 5.0$ m, and then falls uniformly to zero at $x = 8.0$ m, where the pushing stops. Throughout the motion a constant frictional force of 2.0 N acts on the trolley, always opposing its motion; this force is not shown on the graph. The trolley may be treated as a particle. Questions (a) to (e) all refer to this motion. Each is worth one mark and numerical answers should be given to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the total work done by the applied force on the trolley over the whole 8.0 m of the motion.

options.label: A
options.rationale: The work is the area between the graph and the distance axis: a triangle of 6.0 J, a rectangle of 18.0 J and a second triangle of 9.0 J, giving 33.0 J.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This multiplies the greatest force, 6.0 N, by the whole distance, as though the force had been constant at its peak.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This omits the first triangle, counting only the rectangle and the falling part of the graph.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This assumes a mean force of 3.0 N over 8.0 m, which is not the mean height of this particular graph.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the kinetic energy of the trolley at the instant it reaches $x = 8.0$ m, taking the friction into account.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This charges friction over only half the distance, subtracting 8.0 J rather than 16.0 J.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This follows from an applied work of 27.0 J, the value obtained when the first triangle is missed out.

options.label: C
options.rationale: The work done against friction is $2.0 \times 8.0 = 16.0$ J, so the net work is $33.0 - 16.0 = 17.0$ J, which is the kinetic energy gained from rest.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is the work done by the applied force with no allowance for the 16.0 J removed by friction.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the trolley at the instant it reaches $x = 8.0$ m.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This follows the 25.0 J obtained by charging friction over only half the distance.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This uses the full 33.0 J, so it is the speed the trolley would have reached on a frictionless track.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This follows the 11.0 J obtained by missing the first triangle and then subtracting the friction.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the distance from the start at which the kinetic energy of the trolley has its greatest value.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This is where the applied force is greatest, but the force still exceeds friction there, so the trolley is still gaining kinetic energy.

options.label: B
options.rationale: By the end the applied force has fallen to zero while friction has not, so the kinetic energy has already been falling for the last metre.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is halfway along the falling branch, which would be right only if the friction equalled the 3.0 N mean applied force over that branch.

options.label: D
options.rationale: The kinetic energy is the accumulated net work, so it grows while the applied force exceeds the 2.0 N of friction and falls once it drops below it. On the falling branch $F = 16.0 - 2.0x$, which equals 2.0 N at $x = 7.0$ m.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Calculate the power developed by the applied force at the instant the trolley passes $x = 5.0$ m.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This is the work done up to $x = 5.0$ m; power is a rate, not an accumulated amount.

options.label: B
options.rationale: The applied work to $x = 5.0$ m is 24.0 J and friction has taken 10.0 J, leaving 14.0 J, so $v = 3.06$ m s$^{-1}$ there and $P = Fv = 6.0 \times 3.06 = 18.3$ W.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This multiplies 6.0 N by the speed at the end of the motion, 3.37 m s$^{-1}$, rather than the speed at $x = 5.0$ m.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This uses a force of 4.0 N, the mean value of the applied force over the first 5.0 m, instead of its value at that instant.

questions.answer:
**(a) A.** The work done by a force that varies with distance is the area between
its graph and the distance axis, so the region has to be cut into shapes whose areas
are known. It splits into a triangle of area $\tfrac{1}{2}(2.0)(6.0) = 6.0$ J, a
rectangle of area $(3.0)(6.0) = 18.0$ J and a second triangle of area
$\tfrac{1}{2}(3.0)(6.0) = 9.0$ J. Their sum is $6.0 + 18.0 + 9.0 = 33.0$ J. **(A1)**

**(b) C.** Friction acts over the whole 8.0 m and always opposes the motion, so it
does $-2.0 \times 8.0 = -16.0$ J of work. The net work is therefore
$33.0 - 16.0 = 17.0$ J. The trolley started from rest, so by the work-energy theorem
the final kinetic energy is exactly this net work, 17.0 J. **(A1)**

**(c) B.** Setting $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} = 17.0$ J with $m = 3.0$ kg gives
$v = \sqrt{2(17.0)/3.0} = \sqrt{11.33} = 3.37$ m s$^{-1}$. **(A1)**

**(d) D.** The kinetic energy is the *accumulated* net work, so what matters is not
how large the applied force is but whether it exceeds the friction. While $F > 2.0$ N
the trolley keeps gaining energy; once $F < 2.0$ N it starts losing it. On the
falling branch the graph is straight from $(5.0,\ 6.0)$ to $(8.0,\ 0)$, so
$F = 6.0 - 2.0(x - 5.0) = 16.0 - 2.0x$. Setting $F = 2.0$ N gives $x = 7.0$ m. This
lies two metres beyond the point where the applied force is largest, and a metre
before the force disappears. **(A1)**

**(e) B.** Power at an instant is $P = Fv$ with both quantities evaluated at that
instant, so the speed at $x = 5.0$ m is needed first. The applied work to that point
is $6.0 + 18.0 = 24.0$ J and friction has removed $2.0 \times 5.0 = 10.0$ J, so the
kinetic energy there is 14.0 J and $v = \sqrt{2(14.0)/3.0} = 3.06$ m s$^{-1}$. Hence
$P = 6.0 \times 3.06 = 18.3$ W. **(A1)**
questions.markscheme_notes:
One mark per question, no negative marking and no method marks: the key is the answer.
Each distractor is the exact result of a named error, so a wrong option identifies the
error rather than being an arbitrary number.

(a) Accept 33.0 J. An answer of 48.0 J has treated the force as constant at its
maximum value; 27.0 J means the first triangle was left out; 24.0 J means a mean
force of 3.0 N was assumed, and the mean height of this graph is 33.0/8.0 = 4.1 N,
not 3.0 N.

(b) Accept 17.0 J. An answer of 33.0 J shows that the 16.0 J removed by friction was
never subtracted. An answer of 25.0 J has charged friction over half the distance
only, and 11.0 J follows from the incomplete work in part (a).

(c) Accept 3.37 m s$^{-1}$. Do not accept 4.69 m s$^{-1}$, which is the frictionless
answer. A candidate who used 25.0 J in (b) and then computes 4.08 m s$^{-1}$ here has
been consistent but earns no mark, because the value carried forward was itself wrong.

(d) Accept 7.0 m and no other value. This is the discriminating question of the
cluster. An answer of 5.0 m takes the point of greatest force for the point of
greatest energy; 8.0 m assumes the energy is still rising when the force has gone;
6.5 m treats the friction as though it were the 3.0 N mean of the falling branch.

(e) Accept 18.3 W. The commonest error is to reuse the final speed from part (c),
which gives 20.2 W; allow it only if the candidate has also used the speed at the end
in part (c), which it does not. An answer of 24.0 W has confused the work done up to
that point with the rate of doing work.
questions.explanation:
The whole cluster rests on one idea that a single formula cannot carry: a graph of
force against distance is a record of *accumulation*, and the quantity that
accumulates is the net work, not the applied work.

Part (a) is the mechanical one, and the only trap is that the mean height of the
graph is not the average of its endpoint values. Three shapes, three areas, 33.0 J.
Everything afterwards either carries that number forward or loses it.

Part (b) adds the friction, and this is where the cluster first separates candidates.
A constant 2.0 N over 8.0 m is 16.0 J, which is very nearly half of the 33.0 J the
push supplied. Forgetting it is not a slip in method but a change of question: 33.0 J
is the right answer to "how much work did the push do", which is not what was asked.

Part (d) is the question the cluster exists for. The instinct that the kinetic energy
is greatest where the force is greatest is a very natural one, and it is wrong here
because kinetic energy responds to the *net* force integrated over distance, not to
the applied force at a point. Between 5.0 m and 7.0 m the push is weakening but is
still stronger than the friction, so the trolley is still accelerating and still
gaining energy. It is only at 7.0 m, where the falling graph crosses the value of the
friction, that the accumulation turns round. After that the trolley is still moving
forward, and still being pushed, but it is slowing down. The same distinction —
between a quantity and the rate at which that quantity is changing — is what makes
the point of greatest force, the point of greatest speed and the point of greatest
acceleration three different places on the same graph.

Part (e) closes the loop by asking for an instantaneous rate rather than an
accumulated amount. Power is $Fv$ at one instant, so it needs the speed at
$x = 5.0$ m, which is not the speed at $x = 8.0$ m and has to be recovered from the
net work over the first five metres. A candidate who reaches for the final speed has
not made an arithmetic error; they have answered a question about the end of the
motion when asked about the middle of it.

provenance.adaptation: Original cluster. The graph was generated from the same four segment endpoints the answers use, so the drawn line and the arithmetic cannot disagree. The friction was chosen to be constant and to be absent from the figure, so that the turning point of the kinetic energy is a crossing the candidate has to construct rather than a feature of the picture.

verification.method: Every area, every work value, every speed and the power were recomputed in Python from the four segment endpoints used to draw the figure, so that the picture and the arithmetic share one source; each distractor was confirmed to be the exact result of the error it names.
solution_skeleton: cut the force-distance graph into a triangle, a rectangle and a triangle
subtract the work done against the constant friction over the whole distance
convert the remaining net work into a speed with the work-energy theorem
find where the applied force falls to the friction value to locate the energy peak
evaluate the net work up to 5.0 m, then take the product of force and speed there

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Take the kinetic energy to be greatest where the applied force is greatest, which is anywhere between 2.0 m and 5.0 m, and then reuse the speed at the end of the motion when a power at an intermediate point is asked for.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: Kinetic energy is the accumulated net work, so it rises while the applied force exceeds the 2.0 N of friction and falls once it drops below it. On the falling branch the force is F = 16.0 - 2.0x, which reaches 2.0 N at x = 7.0 m: two metres past the force maximum and a metre before the force vanishes. The 6.0 N plateau sets no turning point at all, because what governs the peak is the crossing with the friction, not the size of the push. Power then needs the speed at x = 5.0 m, which is 3.06 m/s from a net work of 14.0 J, and not the 3.37 m/s the trolley has at the end.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: A peak kinetic energy at 5.0 m, where the force is largest, and a power of 20.2 W obtained by multiplying 6.0 N by the final speed of 3.37 m/s.

questions.challenge_mechanism: The hottest state of the gas is not one of the three states drawn on the diagram. Because the isotherms of an ideal gas are rectangular hyperbolae, a straight line across the p-V plane cuts through a whole family of them, so the temperature must reach a maximum somewhere along its interior and come back down. The candidate has to parameterise the line, notice that pV is then a quadratic with a stationary point inside the segment, and evaluate the temperature there rather than at a labelled corner. Every distractor is a reading taken from a point that is on the diagram, so nothing looks wrong.
questions.question: The figure is a pressure-volume diagram for a fixed amount of an ideal gas taken through three successive changes. At state A the pressure is $1.0 \times 10^{5}$ Pa, the volume is $2.0 \times 10^{-3}$ m$^{3}$ and the temperature is 300 K. In the first change the gas expands at constant pressure to state B, where the volume is $6.0 \times 10^{-3}$ m$^{3}$. In the second change it is compressed along the straight line shown to state C, where the pressure is $3.0 \times 10^{5}$ Pa and the volume is $2.0 \times 10^{-3}$ m$^{3}$. In the third change it is cooled at constant volume back to state A. The gas behaves ideally throughout, and the molar gas constant is $R = 8.31$ J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$. Questions (a) to (e) all refer to this gas. Each is worth one mark and numerical answers should be given to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the temperature of the gas when it is at state B.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This divides 300 K by the volume ratio of 3, treating temperature as inversely proportional to volume at constant pressure.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This applies the volume ratio of 3 twice over, as though the pressure had also changed by that factor.

options.label: C
options.rationale: At constant pressure the volume is proportional to the absolute temperature, so tripling the volume from $2.0\times10^{-3}$ to $6.0\times10^{-3}$ m$^{3}$ triples the temperature to 900 K.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This treats the first change as isothermal, but the pressure is held constant while the volume changes, so the temperature cannot stay fixed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the temperature of the gas when it is at state C.

options.label: A
options.rationale: The product $pV$ is 600 Pa m$^{3}$ at C and 200 Pa m$^{3}$ at A, so the temperature is three times 300 K. C is as hot as B even though neither its pressure nor its volume matches B's.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This applies the pressure ratio of 3 and the volume ratio of 3 separately, when only the single product $pV$ fixes the temperature.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This assumes the gas is back at its starting temperature, which would need $pV$ at C to equal $pV$ at A.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is the product $pV = 600$ Pa m$^{3}$ at C read off directly as a temperature, with no reference to the state A.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the amount of substance of gas, in moles, that is present in the container.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This divides by 900 K rather than 300 K, using the temperature of state B or state C in place of the one that is actually stated.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This uses the volume of state B, $6.0\times10^{-3}$ m$^{3}$, in the numerator while keeping the temperature of state A.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is half the correct value, as though the molar gas constant were twice as large as it is.

options.label: D
options.rationale: From $pV = nRT$ at A, $n = (1.0\times10^{5})(2.0\times10^{-3})/(8.31 \times 300) = 0.0802$ mol. State A is the only state whose temperature is given, so it is the one the equation has to be applied to.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the greatest temperature reached by the gas at any point during the three changes.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This is the greatest value of the product $pV$, 800 Pa m$^{3}$, read as a temperature without scaling it against state A.

options.label: B
options.rationale: On the straight segment from B to C the pressure is $p = 4.0\times10^{5} - 5.0\times10^{7}V$, so $pV = 4.0\times10^{5}V - 5.0\times10^{7}V^{2}$, which peaks at $V = 4.0\times10^{-3}$ m$^{3}$ where $pV = 800$ Pa m$^{3}$ and $T = 1200$ K.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is the temperature at the labelled states B and C. The product $pV$ is larger between them than at either end.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This multiplies the greatest pressure by the greatest volume, which is a corner the gas never occupies.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Calculate the temperature of the gas at the point on the change from B to C at which its pressure is $2.50 \times 10^{5}$ Pa.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This is the maximum temperature, which occurs at a pressure of $2.0\times10^{5}$ Pa rather than the one asked for.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is the product $pV = 750$ Pa m$^{3}$ read directly as a temperature, with no scaling against state A.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is the temperature at B and at C, not at a point between them, where the product $pV$ is larger.

questions.answer:
**(a) C.** For a fixed amount of gas at constant pressure, Charles' law gives
$V \propto T$, so $T_{B} = 300 \times (6.0\times10^{-3})/(2.0\times10^{-3}) = 900$ K.
Note that the ratio has to be taken between absolute temperatures and volumes; no
Celsius conversion is involved because both are already absolute. **(A1)**

**(b) A.** The three gas laws combine into $\tfrac{pV}{T} = \text{constant}$, so it
is the product $pV$ that settles the temperature and not either variable alone. At C,
$pV = (3.0\times10^{5})(2.0\times10^{-3}) = 600$ Pa m$^{3}$, and at A,
$pV = 200$ Pa m$^{3}$. The temperature at C is therefore
$300 \times 600/200 = 900$ K. **(A1)**

**(c) D.** Rearranging $pV = nRT$ at A,
$n = (1.0\times10^{5})(2.0\times10^{-3})/(8.31 \times 300) = 200/2493 = 0.0802$ mol.
State A is the only state whose temperature is stated, so it is the only one the
equation can be applied to directly. **(A1)**

**(d) B.** The second change is a straight line from B, at
$(V,\ p) = (6.0\times10^{-3},\ 1.0\times10^{5})$, to C, at
$(2.0\times10^{-3},\ 3.0\times10^{5})$. Its gradient is
$(3.0 - 1.0)\times10^{5}/(2.0 - 6.0)\times10^{-3} = -5.0\times10^{7}$ Pa m$^{-3}$, so
$p = 4.0\times10^{5} - 5.0\times10^{7}V$. The temperature follows $pV$, and
$pV = 4.0\times10^{5}V - 5.0\times10^{7}V^{2}$ is a downward-opening quadratic whose
stationary point satisfies $4.0\times10^{5} = 1.0\times10^{8}V$, giving
$V = 4.0\times10^{-3}$ m$^{3}$ — exactly midway along the segment. There
$p = 2.0\times10^{5}$ Pa, $pV = 800$ Pa m$^{3}$ and
$T = 300 \times 800/200 = 1200$ K. Both endpoints give only 600 Pa m$^{3}$. **(A1)**

**(e) C.** Substituting $p = 2.50\times10^{5}$ Pa into the same line gives
$V = (4.0\times10^{5} - 2.50\times10^{5})/(5.0\times10^{7}) = 3.0\times10^{-3}$
m$^{3}$, so $pV = 750$ Pa m$^{3}$ and $T = 300 \times 750/200 = 1125$ K, which is
1130 K to three significant figures. **(A1)**
questions.markscheme_notes:
One mark per question, no negative marking, and no method marks: the key is the answer.

(a) Accept 900 K. An answer of 100 K has used the volume ratio the wrong way round;
300 K treats the change as isothermal and 1800 K applies the volume ratio twice.

(b) Accept 900 K. Do not accept 2700 K, which applies the pressure ratio and the
volume ratio separately — the single product $pV$ fixes the temperature. An answer
of 600 K has read the product as a temperature. Note for the record that B and C are
at the same temperature, which is why neither of them can be the maximum.

(c) Accept 0.0802 mol. Allow answers in the range 0.0800 to 0.0804. An answer of
0.0267 mol shows the 900 K of part (a) carried into the denominator, and 0.2407 mol
shows the volume of state B carried into the numerator; 0.0401 mol is a factor of two.

(d) Accept 1200 K and no other value. This is the discriminating question of the
cluster, and a candidate who answers 900 K has simply read off the hottest labelled
state. An answer of 800 K has found the correct maximum value of $pV$ and then failed
to scale it, which is a near miss worth crediting in discussion even though it scores
nothing here. Allow 1200 K whether it is reached by differentiating the quadratic, by
completing the square or by tabulating $pV$ along the line.

(e) Accept 1130 K; accept 1125 K. An answer of 750 K has read $pV$ as a temperature,
and 1200 K is the maximum rather than the value at the stated pressure.
questions.explanation:
The single idea behind this cluster is that the temperature of an ideal gas is
proportional to the product $pV$, and that a straight line drawn on a $p$–$V$
diagram is therefore not a line of constant anything.

An isotherm of an ideal gas is a rectangular hyperbola, $pV = \text{constant}$. A
straight segment cuts across a whole family of those hyperbolae. It starts on one,
passes through higher ones, and comes back down to another — so if the two endpoints
happen to lie on the same isotherm, as B and C do here at $pV = 600$ Pa m³, then the
line must have climbed through every isotherm above 600 in between and returned. The
maximum is unavoidable; only its position has to be found.

Finding it is a one-line calculation once the line is written down. With
$p = a + bV$ the product is $pV = aV + bV^{2}$, a parabola, and because the segment
runs downhill $b$ is negative, so the parabola opens downwards and has a genuine
interior maximum at $V = -a/2b$. For these numbers that is $4.0\times10^{-3}$ m³,
which happens to be the midpoint of the segment — but it is the stationary point of
the quadratic that makes it the answer, not any symmetry of the diagram. The
temperature there is 1200 K, a third above the 900 K at either end, and no labelled
point on the figure comes close to marking it.

Two habits make candidates miss this. The first is reading a graph by its vertices:
the instinct that the extreme value of anything must occur at a corner is sound for
a polytope and wrong for a curve. The second is treating the two variables
separately — "the pressure went up by three and the volume by three, so ..." — when
it is only their product that the gas law knows about. Part (b) is built to catch
exactly that, because C has both a larger pressure and a different volume from A, and
only $pV$ gives the right factor of three.

Part (e) is the same computation at a point the candidate chooses, which is why it
sits last: by then the line equation has already been written for part (d), and the
question is whether it can now be used in the other direction.

invert that line at a stated pressure, then convert pV back into a temperature

questions.challenge_mechanism: The cluster is built from two pieces of correct physics that answer questions the stem does not ask. The pendulum period is a real formula and 1.42 s is a real number, but this oscillator's period is fixed by the static extension alone, so neither the 0.600 kg nor the 0.050 m amplitude appears in it at all. Likewise 1.000 m is the correct greatest length for a mass released from the spring's natural length, and this mass was released 0.050 m below equilibrium instead. Because every option is a value a well-taught candidate has seen before, recognising the formula is no help; the stem has to be read for which situation it describes.
questions.question: The figure shows a light spring hanging from a fixed support. On the left the spring is drawn at its unstretched length of 0.500 m. On the right the same spring carries a mass of 0.600 kg and hangs at rest in equilibrium at a length of 0.750 m, so the static extension is 0.250 m. The mass is then pulled down a further 0.050 m below its equilibrium position and released from rest, so that it oscillates vertically about the equilibrium position with an amplitude of 0.050 m. Take $g = 9.81$ m s$^{-2}$, take the spring to be massless and to obey Hooke's law at all times, and ignore air resistance. Questions (a) to (e) all refer to this oscillation. Each is worth one mark and numerical answers should be given to three significant figures.

figure.caption: Two identical springs hanging from supports. The first is shown unloaded at its natural length, 0.500 m. The second carries the 0.600 kg mass and hangs at rest in equilibrium at 0.750 m. The lowest point of the oscillation is not shown.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the period of the vertical oscillation of the mass.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This is twice the correct period, as though the mass completed half an oscillation in each cycle.

options.label: B
options.rationale: In equilibrium $mg = ke$, so $k = 23.5$ N m$^{-1}$ and $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k} = 2\pi\sqrt{0.600/23.5} = 1.00$ s. Equivalently $T = 2\pi\sqrt{e/g}$, which contains neither the mass nor the amplitude.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is $2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$ with the 0.500 m unstretched length, which is the period of a pendulum and not of this oscillator.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is $2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$ with the 0.050 m amplitude, which has no business in either formula: the period is independent of amplitude.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the greatest speed reached by the mass during the oscillation.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This is the amplitude divided by a quarter of the period, which is the mean speed over a quarter cycle and not the greatest speed.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is half the correct value, as though the amplitude were 0.025 m rather than 0.050 m.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is twice the correct value, using twice the amplitude as though the mass travelled the full peak-to-peak distance in a quarter period.

options.label: D
options.rationale: $\omega = 2\pi/T = 6.26$ rad s$^{-1}$, and the greatest speed is $v_{\max} = \omega A = 6.26 \times 0.050 = 0.313$ m s$^{-1}$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the speed of the mass at the instant when it is 0.030 m below its equilibrium position.

options.label: A
options.rationale: The speed obeys $v = \omega\sqrt{A^{2} - x^{2}}$, not a linear rule: $v = 6.26\sqrt{0.050^{2} - 0.030^{2}} = 6.26 \times 0.040 = 0.251$ m s$^{-1}$.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This uses $\omega(A - x)$, treating the speed as though it fell linearly with displacement. It does not; the relation is a quadrature one.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is the greatest speed, which occurs at the equilibrium position and not 0.030 m away from it.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This uses $\omega(A + x)$, which would make the speed larger away from equilibrium than at it.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the greatest length of the spring at any point during the oscillation.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This is the equilibrium length, which the mass passes through rather than turns round at.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This adds twice the amplitude to the equilibrium length, confusing the peak-to-peak travel with the amplitude.

options.label: C
options.rationale: The oscillation is about the equilibrium position, so the length swings between $0.750 - 0.050$ and $0.750 + 0.050$ m; the greatest is 0.800 m.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is the unstretched length plus twice the static extension, which is the greatest length when the mass is released from the spring's natural length. Here it is released 0.050 m below equilibrium, not from the natural length.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of the net force on the mass when it is at the lowest point of the oscillation.

options.label: A
options.rationale: The mass is momentarily at rest there, but a zero velocity is not a zero net force; the net force is what turns it round.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is the weight of the mass. The net force at the lowest point is the excess of the spring force over the weight, not the weight.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is the force exerted by the spring alone, $k(0.250 + 0.050)$; the net force is that minus the weight.

options.label: D
options.rationale: At the lowest point the displacement from equilibrium is the amplitude, so the net force is $kA = 23.5 \times 0.050 = 1.18$ N directed upwards.

questions.answer:
**(a) B.** In equilibrium the spring force balances the weight, so
$mg = ke$ and $k = (0.600)(9.81)/0.250 = 23.5$ N m$^{-1}$. Then
$T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k} = 2\pi\sqrt{0.600/23.5} = 2\pi(0.1597) = 1.00$ s. Substituting
$k = mg/e$ first gives the neater form $T = 2\pi\sqrt{e/g}$, in which the mass has
cancelled: the period depends only on how far the spring hangs down under its own
load, and not on the load or on how far it is then pulled. **(A1)**

**(b) D.** The angular frequency is $\omega = 2\pi/T = 6.26$ rad s$^{-1}$ and the
greatest speed is reached at the equilibrium position, where
$v_{\max} = \omega A = 6.26 \times 0.050 = 0.313$ m s$^{-1}$. The average speed over
a quarter cycle is only 0.199 m s$^{-1}$, because the mass is slow near the ends.
**(A1)**

**(c) A.** Speed and displacement are related by $v^{2} = \omega^{2}(A^{2} - x^{2})$,
so $v = 6.26\sqrt{0.050^{2} - 0.030^{2}} = 6.26\sqrt{0.0016} = 6.26 \times 0.0400 =
0.251$ m s$^{-1}$. The displacement enters squared, so the speed at three fifths of
the amplitude is still four fifths of the maximum, not two fifths of it. **(A1)**

**(d) C.** Simple harmonic motion is motion *about the equilibrium position*, and the
amplitude is measured from there. The length of the spring therefore oscillates
between $0.750 - 0.050 = 0.700$ m and $0.750 + 0.050 = 0.800$ m. The unstretched
length of 0.500 m sets the equilibrium position but plays no part in the excursion.
**(A1)**

**(e) D.** The net force in simple harmonic motion is $F = -m\omega^{2}x$ measured
from equilibrium, and at the lowest point $x = +A = 0.050$ m, so
$|F| = kA = 23.5 \times 0.050 = 1.18$ N upwards. It is worth checking this against the
forces directly: the spring is then stretched by $0.250 + 0.050 = 0.300$ m, so it
pulls up with $23.5 \times 0.300 = 7.06$ N against a weight of 5.89 N, leaving 1.18 N.
**(A1)**

One mark per question, no negative marking, and no method marks: the key is the answer.

(a) Accept 1.00 s. Do not accept 1.42 s, which is a pendulum period built from the
0.500 m unstretched length. An answer of 0.449 s shows the amplitude being used as a
length in the same formula; the period of a simple harmonic oscillator does not
depend on the amplitude.

(b) Accept 0.313 m s⁻¹. An answer of 0.199 m s⁻¹ is the mean speed over a quarter
cycle and is the commonest wrong answer; it is worth drawing the distinction
explicitly if a candidate raises it.

(c) Accept 0.251 m s⁻¹. An answer of 0.125 m s⁻¹ shows a linear rule being used in
place of the quadrature one, which is the specific error this question tests.

(d) Accept 0.800 m. Do not accept 1.000 m. That value is right for a different
experiment — release from the natural length gives a greatest extension of twice the
static extension — and a candidate who offers it has substituted a remembered result
for the situation described.

(e) Accept 1.18 N. An answer of zero confuses a turning point with an equilibrium
point, and the confusion is worth naming: the mass is at rest for an instant precisely
because the net force is at its greatest there. An answer of 7.06 N has computed the
spring force rather than the resultant.
questions.explanation:
A vertical mass–spring system is the standard place where a candidate's two mental
pictures of an oscillator come apart. One picture is of the spring: it has a natural
length, and pulling it down stretches it further. The other is of the oscillation: it
is centred on the equilibrium position, and everything — displacement, speed,
restoring force — is measured from there. The figure draws the two pictures side by
side because the questions only come out right if the second one is used.

Part (a) is where the wrong picture costs most. Reaching for $2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$ is
natural, because it is the formula most candidates have used most often, and with the
0.500 m unstretched length it produces a plausible 1.42 s. But that is the period of a
pendulum, whose restoring force comes from gravity acting on a fixed length. Here the
restoring force comes from the spring, and the period is $2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$. The useful
step is to eliminate $k$ using the static equilibrium condition $mg = ke$, which
collapses the whole thing to $T = 2\pi\sqrt{e/g}$: the period is decided by the
0.250 m the spring sags under its load, and neither the 0.600 kg nor the 0.050 m pull
appears in it at all. That is why a candidate who uses the amplitude as the length gets
0.449 s, and why both wrong answers are wrong for the same reason — they put a length
into the formula that the oscillator's period does not depend on.

Part (d) is the same trap in a different coat. The result that a mass released from a
spring's natural length falls to twice the static extension is real and well taught;
applied here it gives 1.000 m. But that experiment starts at the natural length with
the mass at rest and no oscillation centred anywhere. This one starts 0.050 m below
equilibrium, so the amplitude is 0.050 m and the longest length is 0.800 m. A correct
result from another setup is the most convincing kind of wrong answer, which is exactly
why it is offered.

Part (c) and part (e) close on the two distinctions that survive once the geometry is
right. Speed does not fall linearly with displacement — the relation
$v^{2} = \omega^{2}(A^{2} - x^{2})$ is a quadrature one, so at three fifths of the
amplitude the mass still has four fifths of its maximum speed. And a turning point is
not an equilibrium point: at the lowest point the velocity is zero because the net
force is largest, 1.18 N upwards, which is what sends the mass back.

form the period from T = 2*pi*sqrt(m/k) and eliminate k to get 2*pi*sqrt(e/g)
take the greatest speed as the product of angular frequency and amplitude
use the quadrature relation between speed and displacement, not a linear one
add the amplitude to the equilibrium length and take the net force as k times the displacement

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the lowest frequency at which the air column in pipe P resonates.

options.label: A
options.rationale: A closed end forces a displacement node and an open end an antinode, so a quarter of a wavelength fills the pipe: $\lambda = 4L = 3.40$ m and $f = v/\lambda = 100$ Hz.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is $v/2L$, the fundamental of a pipe open at both ends, not of one closed at one end.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This takes the length of the pipe to be exactly one wavelength.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This takes half the length of the pipe to be one wavelength.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the third lowest frequency at which the air column in pipe P resonates.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This is an even multiple of the fundamental. A pipe closed at one end cannot sustain any even harmonic, so it is not a resonance at all.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is the second harmonic, which is absent from this pipe's series altogether.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Only the odd harmonics of 100 Hz can form, because the closed end must be a node and the open end an antinode. The series is 100, 300, 500, 700 Hz, and the third of those is 500 Hz.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is the third harmonic, $3f_{1}$, which is the second lowest resonance and not the third.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the lowest frequency at which the air column in pipe Q resonates.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This is the fundamental of the closed pipe; opening the far end raises the fundamental by a factor of two.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This uses $\lambda = 4L$, the closed-pipe condition, for a pipe that has no closed end.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This takes the length of the pipe to be exactly one wavelength.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Both ends are open, so both are antinodes and half a wavelength fills the pipe: $\lambda = 2L = 1.70$ m and $f = 340/1.70 = 200$ Hz.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the length of a pipe that is open at both ends and whose lowest resonant frequency equals the lowest resonant frequency of pipe P.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Equating the two fundamentals, $v/2L_{\text{open}} = v/4L_{\text{closed}}$, gives $L_{\text{open}} = 2L_{\text{closed}} = 1.70$ m.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This assumes the same fundamental needs the same length, and misses the factor of two between the two boundary conditions.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This carries the ordering across from part (c): the closed pipe is lower at a given length, so it is taken to be shorter at a given pitch. The ranking reverses.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is the wavelength of 100 Hz sound in air, not the length of pipe that resonates at that frequency.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Calculate the distance between adjacent nodes of the standing wave in pipe P when it is resonating at 500 Hz.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This is a quarter of a wavelength, the separation between a node and the adjacent antinode.

options.label: B
options.rationale: At 500 Hz the wavelength is $v/f = 340/500 = 0.680$ m, and adjacent nodes are half a wavelength apart, so 0.340 m.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is the wavelength; adjacent nodes are separated by half of it.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is the length of the pipe, which is five quarters of a wavelength at this frequency.

questions.answer:
**(a) A.** The closed end must be a displacement node and the open end a displacement
antinode, and the shortest way to join a node to an antinode is a quarter of a
wavelength. So $\lambda = 4L = 4(0.850) = 3.40$ m and $f = v/\lambda = 340/3.40 =
100$ Hz. **(A1)**

**(b) C.** Each successive mode adds another half wavelength between the node and the
antinode, which adds $2f_{1}$ to the frequency rather than $f_{1}$. The series is
therefore $f_{1},\ 3f_{1},\ 5f_{1},\ \ldots$, that is 100, 300, 500, 700 Hz. The third
lowest of these is 500 Hz, which is the fifth harmonic. **(A1)**

**(c) D.** With both ends open, both are antinodes, and the shortest way to join an
antinode to an antinode is half a wavelength. So $\lambda = 2L = 1.70$ m and
$f = 340/1.70 = 200$ Hz, an octave above pipe P of the same length. **(A1)**

**(d) A.** The two fundamentals are $v/4L$ for the closed pipe and $v/2L$ for the open
one. Setting them equal, $v/2L_{\text{open}} = v/4(0.850)$, gives
$L_{\text{open}} = 2(0.850) = 1.70$ m. The open pipe has to be twice as long to sound
as low. **(A1)**

**(e) B.** At 500 Hz the wavelength in air is $\lambda = v/f = 340/500 = 0.680$ m. In
any standing wave the nodes are spaced half a wavelength apart, so the separation is
0.340 m. As a check, the pipe holds $0.850/0.680 = 1.25$ wavelengths, which is five
quarters — exactly what the fifth harmonic of a stopped pipe requires. **(A1)**
questions.markscheme_notes:
One mark per question, no negative marking, and no method marks: the key is the answer.

(a) Accept 100 Hz. An answer of 200 Hz has applied the open-pipe condition to a closed
pipe; 400 Hz and 800 Hz take the pipe length to be one wavelength and half a
wavelength respectively.

(b) Accept 500 Hz and no other value. This question separates the count of resonances
from the harmonic number, and 300 Hz is the answer it exists to catch: that is the
third harmonic but only the second resonance. Do not accept 400 Hz under any
circumstances — it is an even multiple of the fundamental and a stopped pipe cannot
resonate there at all.

(c) Accept 200 Hz. An answer of 100 Hz has carried the closed-pipe value across
unchanged; 50.0 Hz uses the closed-pipe condition on a pipe with no closed end.

(d) Accept 1.70 m. An answer of 0.425 m is the discriminating error: it takes the
ordering from part (c), where the closed pipe is the lower of the two at equal length,
and assumes the closed pipe must therefore be the shorter at equal pitch. It is the
other way round. An answer of 3.40 m has given the wavelength rather than the length.

(e) Accept 0.340 m. An answer of 0.680 m has given the wavelength instead of half of
it, and 0.170 m is the node-to-antinode distance.
questions.explanation:
Everything in this cluster comes from two sentences: a closed end is a displacement
node, an open end is a displacement antinode. Everything else is counting how many
quarter-wavelengths fit between them.

For the stopped pipe the count is odd, always. The fundamental fits one quarter; each
mode above it adds a node–antinode pair, which is a further half wavelength, so the
series runs $1, 3, 5, 7$ quarters and the frequencies run $f_{1}, 3f_{1}, 5f_{1},
7f_{1}$. Two consequences get confused in examinations and both are tested here. The
first is that the harmonic number and the position in the list are not the same thing:
500 Hz is the third resonance and the fifth harmonic. The second is that the missing
even harmonics are not merely absent but *forbidden* — a standing wave with an even
number of quarter-wavelengths would need the far end to be both a node and an
antinode. That is why 400 Hz is not a quiet resonance but no resonance at all.

The open pipe has no such restriction. Both ends are antinodes, so the count is even —
$2, 4, 6$ quarters — and every harmonic is present. At the same length its fundamental
is twice the stopped pipe's, which is the organ builder's reason for using stopped
pipes: a stopped pipe gives you an octave for half the metal.

Part (d) is where the cluster turns. The comparison has been made once with length
held fixed, and now it is made again with frequency held fixed, and the two answers
point opposite ways. At equal length the stopped pipe is lower, 100 Hz against 200 Hz.
At equal frequency the stopped pipe is shorter, 0.850 m against 1.70 m. The algebra
says this without any risk of confusion — equating $v/4L_{c}$ with $v/2L_{o}$ gives
$L_{o} = 2L_{c}$ — but a candidate reasoning from the remembered ordering rather than
from the expression will halve where they should double. That is a general hazard of
comparative reasoning, not a fact about pipes: the ranking of two things is a property
of the comparison, not of the things, and it can reverse when the quantity held fixed
changes.

Part (e) is a small check that the picture still makes sense. At 500 Hz the wavelength
is 0.680 m and the pipe is 1.25 wavelengths long, which is the fifth harmonic of a
stopped pipe exactly as part (b) claimed.

The length 0.850 m with a sound speed of 340 m/s was chosen so that the closed fundamental is exactly 100 Hz, which makes the odd-harmonic series and the node spacing both clean, and so that the equal-pitch length of 1.70 m is a simple doubling rather than an awkward number. The figure draws only the geometry and the end conditions, so the boundary conditions have to be known rather than read off a drawn standing wave.

verification.method: Both fundamental expressions, the odd-harmonic series, the equal-pitch length and the node spacing were recomputed in Python and cross-checked against the fraction of a wavelength each mode occupies; each distractor was confirmed to be the exact result of the error its rationale names.
solution_skeleton: fix the boundary condition at each end and the fraction of a wavelength it forces
list the allowed modes of the closed pipe as the odd multiples of its fundamental
separate the position of a resonance in the list from its harmonic number
equate the two fundamental expressions and solve for the length that is asked for
turn the resonant frequency into a wavelength, then halve it for the node spacing

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Carry the ordering from the first comparison into the second: the closed pipe is the lower pitched of the two at equal length, so at equal pitch it must be the shorter, giving 0.425 m rather than 1.70 m.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: At equal length the closed pipe's fundamental is v/4L = 100 Hz against the open pipe's v/2L = 200 Hz, so the closed pipe is an octave lower. Equating the two fundamentals instead gives v/4L_closed = v/2L_open, so L_open = 2 L_closed = 1.70 m. The pipe that is lower at a given length is the longer one at a given pitch, and the ranking reverses with the quantity held fixed. Separately, the closed end deletes every even harmonic, so the third resonance is 500 Hz and not the 300 Hz third harmonic.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: E.3 (Radioactive decay: activity and the decay constant, the half-life, the exponential decay of activity and of the number of undecayed nuclei, and the correction of a measured count rate for background radiation)
questions.topic: Theme E: Nuclear and quantum physics
questions.subtopic: E.3 Radioactive decay: how a constant background changes every fold-change in a measured count rate
questions.challenge_mechanism: The exponential law governs the activity and governs nothing else in this cluster. What the detector records is the activity scaled by an efficiency and then shifted by a constant, and a shift does not decay. So the recorded rate does not fall by the same factor as the activity, does not halve after one half-life, and never falls below the background however long the wait. Every distractor is the number the exponential alone would give, and every one of them forgets a quantity that was stated once, in one sentence, and appears in no formula.
questions.question: A radioactive source is placed in front of a detector. With the source in position the detector records 960 counts during a measuring interval of 120 s. With the source removed, but with the detector, its shielding and the room exactly as they were, it records 120 counts during a second interval of the same length. The detector registers 4.0% of the decays that occur in the source; the remainder are missed because the radiation is emitted in all directions and much of it never reaches the detector. The source consists of a single nuclide of half-life 12 h and emits no other radiation. Questions (a) to (e) all refer to this arrangement. Each is worth one mark and numerical answers should be given to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the background-corrected count rate at the start of the measurements, in counts per second.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This is the background rate on its own, which is what has to be removed, not what is left.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This converts the gross count to a rate per second but the background count to a rate per minute, so the two are not in the same units when they are subtracted.

options.label: C
options.rationale: The gross rate is $960/120 = 8.00$ s$^{-1}$ and the background rate is $120/120 = 1.00$ s$^{-1}$, so the corrected rate is 7.00 s$^{-1}$.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is the gross rate with the background left in; the detector did not stop counting when the source was taken away.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the activity of the source at the start of the measurements, in becquerels.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This divides by 0.10 rather than 0.040, treating a 4.0% efficiency as though it were ten per cent.

options.label: B
options.rationale: The corrected rate of 7.00 s$^{-1}$ is 4.0% of the activity, so $A = 7.00/0.040 = 175$ Bq.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This divides the gross rate by the efficiency, so the background has been counted as though it came from the source.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is the count rate itself. Count rate and activity differ by the detecting efficiency, which is far from unity here.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the count rate that the detector will record, in counts per second, 24 h after the start of the measurements.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This quarters the rate that was recorded at the start. The activity quarters, but the background does not, so the recorded rate cannot.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is the background-corrected rate after 24 h. The detector has no way of telling a decay from a background event, so it records both.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This halves the recorded rate as though 24 h were one half-life. It is two, and the background does not decay in any case.

options.label: D
options.rationale: 24 h is two half-lives, so the activity falls to $175/4 = 43.75$ Bq, giving a corrected rate of $43.75 \times 0.040 = 1.75$ s$^{-1}$. The detector still records the background on top of it, so the rate is 2.75 s$^{-1}$.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the time, in hours, at which the count rate recorded by the detector has fallen to one half of the rate it recorded at the start of the measurements.

options.label: A
options.rationale: The recorded rate starts at 8.00 s$^{-1}$, so it halves at 4.00 s$^{-1}$, which means a corrected rate of 3.00 s$^{-1}$. Solving $7.00 \times 2^{-t/12} = 3.00$ gives $t = 12\log_{2}(7/3) = 14.7$ h.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is one half-life, which halves the activity. The recorded rate is the activity plus a fixed background, so it takes longer than one half-life to halve.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is half a half-life, as though the background made the recorded rate fall faster than the activity. It makes it fall more slowly.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is two half-lives, which quarters the activity rather than halving the recorded rate.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Calculate the number of nuclei of the nuclide present in the source at the start of the measurements.

options.label: A
options.rationale: This follows from an activity of 100 Bq, which is not a value any part of this cluster produces.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is one fifth of the correct value, following from a decay constant five times too large, as if the half-life had been given in hours and used as seconds.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This follows from the activity of 200 Bq obtained in part (b) when the background is not subtracted.

questions.answer:
**(a) C.** Both totals have to become rates before they can be compared, and both
were taken over the same 120 s. The gross rate is $960/120 = 8.00$ s$^{-1}$ and the
background rate is $120/120 = 1.00$ s$^{-1}$, so the rate due to the source alone is
$8.00 - 1.00 = 7.00$ s$^{-1}$. **(A1)**

**(b) B.** The detector registers only 4.0% of the decays, so the corrected count rate
is 0.040 of the activity: $A = 7.00/0.040 = 175$ Bq. The activity is a property of the
source and does not depend on how well it is being watched, which is why the efficiency
has to be divided out. **(A1)**

**(c) D.** Twenty-four hours is two half-lives, so the activity falls by a factor of
four to $175/4 = 43.75$ Bq. The corrected count rate is then
$43.75 \times 0.040 = 1.75$ s$^{-1}$. But the detector cannot distinguish a decay from
a background event, so it records $1.75 + 1.00 = 2.75$ s$^{-1}$. The recorded rate has
fallen by a factor of $8.00/2.75 = 2.91$, not 4. **(A1)**

**(d) A.** The recorded rate starts at 8.00 s$^{-1}$ and has to fall to 4.00 s$^{-1}$,
which means the corrected rate must fall from 7.00 to 3.00 s$^{-1}$ — and the
background has to be removed before this can be seen. Solving
$7.00 \times 2^{-t/12} = 3.00$ gives $2^{t/12} = 7/3$, so
$t = 12\log_{2}(7/3) = 12 \times 1.222 = 14.7$ h. The recorded rate takes almost
fifteen hours to halve even though the activity halves in twelve. **(A1)**

**(e) C.** The half-life must be in seconds before it gives a decay constant in
reciprocal seconds: $\lambda = \ln 2/(12 \times 3600) = 1.60\times10^{-5}$ s$^{-1}$.
Then $A = \lambda N$ gives $N = 175/1.60\times10^{-5} = 1.09\times10^{7}$ nuclei.
**(A1)**
questions.markscheme_notes:
One mark per question, no negative marking, and no method marks: the key is the answer.

(a) Accept 7.00 s⁻¹. An answer of 8.00 s⁻¹ has left the background in and 1.00 s⁻¹ has
kept only the background; 6.00 s⁻¹ mixes a per-second rate with a per-minute one.

(b) Accept 175 Bq. An answer of 200 Bq shows the gross rate being used, so the
background has been treated as decays from the source. An answer of 7.00 Bq has
confused a count rate with an activity.

(c) Accept 2.75 s⁻¹. This is the discriminating question. Do not accept 2.00 s⁻¹,
which applies the decay factor to the recorded rate, and do not accept 1.75 s⁻¹, which
is the corrected rate with the background not put back.

(d) Accept 14.7 h; accept 14.6 h or 14.8 h from a rounded logarithm. An answer of
12.0 h has halved the activity rather than the recorded rate, and is the commonest
wrong answer. An answer of 6.00 h has the background acting in the wrong direction.

(e) Accept 1.09 × 10⁷. Allow answers in the range 1.08 × 10⁷ to 1.10 × 10⁷. An answer
of 2.18 × 10⁶ usually means the half-life was used in seconds without converting from
hours, giving a decay constant sixty times too large; a fifth suggests a different
slip, and is worth checking individually.
questions.explanation:
There are two quantities in this cluster and the whole difficulty is keeping them
apart. The first is the activity of the source, 175 Bq. It obeys $A = \lambda N$ and
$A = A_{0}e^{-\lambda t}$, it halves every 12 h, and nothing that happens in the
laboratory changes it. The second is the count rate the detector records. It is
$0.040A + b$, where $b$ is the background, and it is the only one of the two that
anyone actually measures.

The background is a shift, not a scaling, and that is the entire point. Multiplying by
0.040 commutes with the exponential: the corrected count rate falls by exactly the same
factor as the activity, so over 24 h it really does quarter, from 7.00 to 1.75 s⁻¹.
Adding the background afterwards does not commute with anything. So the recorded rate
falls from 8.00 to 2.75 s⁻¹, a factor of 2.91 rather than 4, and the difference
between 2.91 and 4 is entirely the extra 1.00 s⁻¹ that was there at the start and is
still there at the end.

Part (d) turns the same observation into the question it is really about. If the
recorded rate halved after one half-life, then adding a constant would have no effect
on a fold-change, which is false: a constant offset always slows a fall towards it. The
recorded rate is heading for 1.00 s⁻¹, not for zero, so it covers the first half of its
fall more slowly than the second half of it in proportional terms — and it takes 14.7 h
rather than 12 h. Notice that the answer is *longer* than a half-life. An offset that
does not decay can only ever delay a fall, never hasten it, so any candidate who
produces a time shorter than 12 h has made an error of direction as well as of
arithmetic.

Part (b) and part (e) are the two conversions that bracket the calculation, and both
are places where a quantity changes units. Turning a count rate into an activity
divides by 0.040, because a detector that sees one decay in twenty-five is not a
detector that sees one decay in ten. Turning a half-life into a decay constant requires
the half-life in seconds, because $\lambda$ is a rate; 12 h is 43 200 s, not 12 s.
Neither step is difficult and both are routinely skipped.

One practical note worth making explicit: the background was measured with the source
removed but everything else unchanged. That is what makes $b$ the same 1.00 s⁻¹ in
every part. If the shielding or the geometry had moved between the two measurements,
none of the subtraction would be valid — the correction is only as good as the claim
that the two intervals differ in exactly one respect.

verification.method: Both rates, the activity, the decayed activity, the halving time and the number of nuclei were recomputed in Python, including the logarithms; each distractor was confirmed to be the exact result of the error its rationale names.
solution_skeleton: turn both totals of counts into rates and subtract the background from the gross rate
divide the corrected rate by the detecting efficiency to recover the activity
decay the activity over the elapsed time, convert it back and add the background again
set the recorded rate to half its initial value and solve for the time in the exponent
form the decay constant from the half-life in seconds, then divide the activity by it

difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The recorded rate is not proportional to the activity, because the background is added after the efficiency scaling rather than before it. Scaling by 0.040 commutes with the exponential, so the corrected rate does quarter, from 7.00 to 1.75 per second; adding the 1.00 per second background does not, so the recorded rate falls from 8.00 to 2.75, a factor of 2.91 and not 4. The same offset puts the halving of the recorded rate at 14.7 h rather than 12 h: a constant that does not decay can only delay a fall towards it, never hasten one.
